paper_title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Long-running agents often make choices that change both the resources available for future work and the obligations they will need to meet (Brehmer, 1992; Kumar et al., 2026; Han et al., 1 2026). The value of these choices depends on how later decisions maintain or revise the resource arrangements they create (Sun et al., 2023; You et al., 2026). Consider rental manager with one tent available today. Renting it earns immediate income but may leave it unavailable for more valuable trip later. Holding it preserves that opportunity, whose arrival and value remain uncertain. Once the manager accepts future booking, an intervening rental also affects an existing obligation: serving both customers requires enough time for the tent to return, be cleaned, and become ready again. Later rental decisions must therefore weigh new opportunities against the capacity needed for commitments already made (Zhang and Cheung, 2022). Recent business benchmarks evaluate agents through continuing operations, including purchasing, pricing, and customer management (Andon Labs, 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b), as well as contract selection and financing decisions with lasting consequences (He et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026). Less attention has been given to how agents jointly maintain the feasibility of their own commitments and reassess resource allocations as opportunities change. To address this gap, we introduce OutfitterBench, benchmark in which agents manage simulated outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days. Its design draws on work linking planning with the evaluation of alternatives (Bratman et al., 1988) and examining how existing plans change the value of new options (Horty and Pollack, 2001). We focus on two coupled demands. Intertemporal feasibility maintenance requires keeping changing asset states, accepted work, and subsequent actions compatible. Intertemporal resource valuation and reallocation requires comparing competing uses of equipmenttime and capital when forming commitments and revisiting existing allocations. In OutfitterBench, advance reservations and uncertain walk-in demand draw from shared fleet Figure 1: Business value created over the season, averaged equally over two world seeds for each agent. Curves use contract-adjusted economic value relative to the initial shop, accounting for equipment and outstanding obligations. Labels on the right report mean official net value creation (V ) at day 214. Shading marks the 14-day automatic settlement period. Calendar provides fixed-policy reference between the highestand lower-performing agents. whose availability changes through rental, return, cleaning, and maintenance. New rentals can undermine the supply supporting earlier bookings; protecting those bookings can exclude more valuable uses. The agent chooses bookings and prices, arranges supply, and limits walk-in use. It can negotiate changes or cancel booking at compensation cost. Purchases and sales reshape future supply; once the fixed equipment-capital ceiling binds, new investment may require replacing existing assets. The environment combines product catalog derived from Taobao listings and historical Beijing weather with models of customer demand and equipment operations. The objective is to maximize terminal value: cash plus eligible equipment resale value minus outstanding liabilities. We compare 7 model configurations with public-information rule policy on the same 2 world seeds. Figure 1 summarizes the resulting value paths. The rule policy outperforms several agents, while only the leading agent exceeds it in both worlds. Agents can serve more bookings and still lose business value. Some agents repeatedly schedule equipment without allowing for turnaround; stronger runs sometimes overlook other affected commitments when preparing supply across days. Reliable fulfillment can also coexist with lower rents for comparable bookings, investment assessments that fail to guide later asset choices, and protection limits that exclude usable rental intervals. The leading agent more often connects supply preparation with these economic comparisons, although local counterfactual tests reveal remaining opportunities for more profitable equipment use. Taken together, these findings reveal limits in agents ability to keep successive decisions compatible and to reassess resource allocations as the value of competing uses changes. Our contributions are threefold: 1. benchmark for long-horizon resource allocation and commitment coordination. We introduce OutfitterBench, continuing rental environment that couples dynamic asset availability, agent-chosen future obligations, and uncertain opportunities under long-term business-value objective. agents evaluate 2. comparative evaluation of LLM agents. publicWe information rule-based baseline on matched world seeds, revealing substantial differences in long-term business value, with several agents underperforming the baseline. against 3. systematic analysis of intertemporal decisions. We combine trajectory analy2 sis with state-based diagnostics, matchedbooking comparisons, and local counterfactual tests. The analysis identifies failures to carry constraints across decisions, weaker returns from comparable commitments, and gaps between investment assessments and subsequent resource choices. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Interactive and Long-Horizon Agent Benchmarks. Interactive benchmarks evaluate tool use, policy adherence, and actions with observable consequences (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024). Workplace and cross-session workflows extend these demands to coordinating tools and using information from earlier interactions (Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), while games and discovery environments examine sustained exploration, strategic decisions, and adaptation to evolving states or unfamiliar rules (Paglieri et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025). Continuing business simulations connect repeated operating decisions to long-term outcomes. Vending-Bench 2, FoodTruck Bench, RetailBench, and related e-commerce environments couple sourcing, pricing, inventory, and cash flow (Andon Labs, 2025; FoodTruck Bench, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Project and enterprise simulations examine contract selection, investment, and ongoing services (He et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026), while multi-firm economies additionally study negotiation and market interaction (Sugiura et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Across these settings, earlier decisions shape the opportunities and constraints of subsequent action. Planning and Commitment Coordination. Maintaining plan requires checking how actions and new observations affect the conditions for subsequent steps (Ghallab et al., 2016). Planning evaluations test plan generation, verification, and replanning (Valmeekam et al., 2023). Feedback-driven methods revise plans when observations depart from expectations (Sun et al., 2023), while coordination frameworks explicitly manage execution dependencies and detect stale joint plans (You et al., 2026). Coordination can also depend on agreements formed during earlier interactions. SCARCE studies how agents with separate objectives negotiate access to shared execution resources and develop agreements and norms that persist across tasks (Kumar et al., 2026). OutfitterBench examines different coordination problem: whether manager can keep customer commitments compatible with changing resource availability and subsequent allocations. Intertemporal Resource Allocation. resource decision affects both current returns and what remains available for later work. Inventory control studies examine ordering under demand shifts and uncertain lead times (Baek et al., 2026). When agents also choose which work to accept, resource allocation and commitment formation become linked. In YC-Bench, accepted projects draw on fixed workforce, with progress accumulating toward project deadlines; taking on additional work can overcommit shared employee effort (He et al., 2026). CEO-Bench links growth and investment to the capacity needed for continuing service (Chen et al., 2026), while EnterpriseArena examines how financing timing and scale affect future liquidity under delayed settlement and changing economic conditions (Han et al., 2026). Reusable-resource allocation makes the duration of occupancy part of the economic decision: serving one customer temporarily removes capacity from other potential uses (Zhang and Cheung, 2022). Whereas project work can accumulate toward completion before deadline, rental commitments require reusable capacity during specified future service intervals. OutfitterBench examines how agents keep such arrangements feasible while reassessing which resource uses to retain or revise.

sections.title: 3 OutfitterBench
sections.content: OutfitterBench simulates an outdoor-equipment rental business. Rental provides setting for reusable-resource allocation: accepting business commits capacity before later demand is known (Chen et al., 2017; Zhang and Cheung, 2022). To study feasibility maintenance and resource valuation together, we design the environment around three interacting features. First, outdoor trips require complementary equipment to be ready together, while rental, return, and servicing change its availability. Agents must keep accepted bookings compatible with evolving supply and subsequent uses. Second, customers com3 pete for shared rental capacity (Savin et al., 2005): reservations and uncertain walk-ins draw on the same fleet. Prices and capacity protection determine what commitments earn and which opportunities remain available. Third, agents can revise commitments and change fleet composition, but customer response delays, cancellation compensation, and resale losses make adjustments costly. Once the equipment-capital ceiling binds, new investment may require replacing existing assets. We construct the product catalog from Taobao listings and use historical Beijing weather to model demand and operating conditions. Customer behavior and equipment operations follow explicit rules and probabilistic models. Figure 2 gives an overview of the environment. 3.1 Task, Interaction, and Objective season comprises 200 manager-decision days followed by 14 automatic settlement days, during which outstanding rentals, service work, and liabilities settle after new business ends. The objective is to maximize terminal business value: cash plus eligible equipment resale value, less outstanding liabilities. Rent generates income, while procurement, servicing, operating expenses, and customer compensation create costs. Section 4.3 defines the score and reported value gain. Each morning, the environment processes deliveries, service work, returns, and eligible pickups. The agent receives an inbox and can query records, set prices, buy or sell equipment, arrange servicing, and handle bookings. At closing, the environment resolves outstanding pickup issues, serves walk-ins, charges daily costs, and advances the day. Each day starts fresh model session. Business records persist, and the agent can maintain retrievable notes and handoff for the next day. Observations include finances, transactions, asset and contract states, service schedules, customer feedback, and the public calendar and weather forecast. Customer preferences are partly revealed through interactions; future requests and operating outcomes remain uncertain.

sections.title: 3.2 Customer Demand and Commitments
sections.content: Reservations and walk-ins compete for the same fleet, linking current admissions to capacity available for later bookings. Both channels originate from common pool of potential outings. For each intended outing day and trip type (overnight camping, picnic outings, or lightweight trips), the simulator samples the number of potential customer parties: Nk,d Poisson(λk,d). (1) The rate λk,d varies with season and calendar. Weekends and public holidays concentrate demand; school holidays also increase weekday activity. Each party is assigned channel and, for reservations, booking lead time. Advance customers decide whether to submit request using the forecast available that day for their trip; walk-ins respond to arrival-day weather. The agent sees the same public forecast. For each outing, we sample party composition and rental duration by trip type and calendar, then generate required and optional equipment needs. Public service profiles translate these needs into suitable products and quantities using functional guarantees, such as temperature suitability, and peritem capacities, such as sleeping places. Budget and preference parameters come from predefined scenario distributions, allowing parties with similar needs to value equipment and rental convenience differently. Equipment choices within reservation share budget and price-sensitivity parameters, with preferences also varying by category. For advance inquiries, we use random-utility model (Train, 2009) to compare complete rental plans with buying equipment, using gear already available to the party, or abandoning the trip. products functional fit and quality contribute to both purchase and rental utility (Lancaster, 1966). Ownership benefits, service convenience, payments, and the rental deposit then affect the relative appeal of the alternatives. quoted plan is acceptable when its utility exceeds that of the outside alternatives. These alternatives therefore constrain what customers are willing to pay for rental plan. Walk-ins choose required equipment first; optional choices depend on those selections. Advance requests specify equipment requirements, trip lengths, and permitted pickup dates. We include two forms to examine how agents choose which work to undertake and on what terms. Fixedterm offers provide customer-approved configurations and rents; the agent selects plan and date or declines. For manager-priced inquiries, it proposes configurations and prices for customer approval. Equipment choices and prices shape both the return from commitment and the capacity left for other opportunities, linking pricing with 4 Figure 2: The OutfitterBench rental shop combines two demand channels with reusable equipment fleet. The agent manages bookings, walk-in prices and occupancy limits, and equipment investment using business records, public forecasts, and customer feedback. Calendar and weather jointly shape demand and the timing of equipment reuse, while fixed equipment-capital ceiling constrains fleet expansion. Performance after 200 decision days and 14 automatic settlement days is terminal cash plus eligible equipment resale value, less outstanding liabilities. resource allocation (Bitran and Caldentey, 2003; Talluri and van Ryzin, 2004). Customer approval can directly confirm quoted booking. Confirmation fixes products, quantities, dates, and prices as obligations that the agent must support or revise through later decisions. Walk-ins are served automatically at closing using posted prices and ready equipment. The agent controls new walk-in occupancy through productand date-specific limits on how many units those rentals can occupy. Walk-in rentals can extend into future booking windows, and new reservations can overlap earlier bookings. Through both channels, the agent commits capacity before knowing which later requests will arrive or what they will be worth. To support learning from experience, the environment provides transaction histories, unfilled walk-in requests, and occasional noisy feedback on declined quotations, including concerns about price or equipment fit. Together with public product attributes, these records give agents evidence about how customer responses vary with equipment, prices, and trip conditions.

sections.title: 3.3 Shared Capacity and Resource Allocation
sections.content: Meeting accepted commitments requires coordinating complementary assets whose readiness depends on prior rentals and shared turnaround capacity. The shop starts with 27 physical assets and can purchase from 46-product catalog of tents, sleeping equipment, and picnic supplies. Different parties can draw on overlapping sets of suitable products, while their functional requirements limit substitution. booking may require several equipment types together, so shortage can prevent complete fulfillment even when other equipment is idle. Confirmed products remain binding unless the customer authorizes change. Each unit has its own condition, usage history, and operational status. Once rented, unit becomes available again only after returning and completing required cleaning, repair, or maintenance. Returns enter shared, capacity-limited cleaning queue and become available no earlier than the next day. Cleaning workload determines both the cleaning charge and the demand placed on the shared 5 Figure 3: Competing uses of single tent. The new request overlaps confirmed booking, whereas walk-in rental could fit before it with one-day margin after cleaning. Late return or servicing delays could eliminate this margin. Solid and dashed outlines denote confirmed and candidate rentals, respectively. queue. The shared queue can delay readiness for other orders, even across equipment types or nonoverlapping rental intervals. compares the value of fulfillment with that of releasing capacity, accounting for agreed rent, further preparation, and the cost of changing course. Calendar and weather effects connect demand with these constraints. Holidays can bring more and longer trips while making renters more likely to extend their use; weather exposure changes cleaning workloads. Updated forecasts can prompt rescheduling or cancellation. Public information and operating history help anticipate these patterns, although individual outcomes remain uncertain. The agent can accept bookings against expected deliveries, returns, and service completions, with units assigned at pickup. Confirmation records the agreed obligations without checking future capacity; the agent must arrange supply and keep later allocations compatible with existing bookings. Walk-in limits can protect bookings but also exclude rentals that would leave equipment ready again before the booked pickup. Figure 3 illustrates these competing uses. As conditions change, the agent can reassess how and whether to support commitment. Before pickup, it can propose revisions; customers respond the next day, and accepted terms take effect when the agent applies them. Substitutions or reduced delivery at pickup require authorization. Alternatively, the agent can cancel, refund unearned payments, and pay compensation that increases as pickup approaches. Waiting may improve information but leave fewer adjustment options. The agent Fleet investments compete for fixed equipmentcapital allowance. Purchases require cash and must satisfy: Bt + It Kmax, (2) where Bt is the historical acquisition cost still counted against the ceiling, and It is the cost of accepted inbound orders. Sale or disposal releases capital basis the next morning; until then, that basis remains in Bt. Revenue adds cash without raising Kmax. Owned equipment also incurs daily holding charges. Dealer resale value starts at 55% of purchase cost for intact, unused equipment and declines with condition and wear. When the ceiling binds, new purchases may require replacing existing assets. The agent compares the future uses of current and replacement assets, accounting for resale losses, holding costs, delivery waits, and existing booking obligations.

sections.title: 3.4 Data Sources and Parameterization
sections.content: We use DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 as an auxiliary model to clean and structure product information from Taobao listings. Specifications provide functional attributes and per-item capacities; listing prices inform procurement costs and customers purchase alternatives, with selected adjustments recorded as benchmark settings. Products are matched to service profiles through rules on 6 these attributes. The model also estimates productlevel durability and cleaning workload from listed materials and construction details. Shared operating and cost rules translate these priors into wear accumulated through rental days and turnovers, cleaning-queue workloads, and service charges. Before freezing the data, we apply deterministic checks to verify profile membership against product specifications, validate capacities, and confirm compatible profile for each rental product. Customer budget and preference distributions, together with behavioral response parameters, are specified as benchmark settings. Historical Beijing weather is replayed by month and day. We synthesize public forecasts by perturbing temperatures and weather categories using lead-time-dependent error settings. The demand and operating models use this shared weather sequence and the public calendar. Random draws are indexed by event and world seed to support reproducible simulation. Appendices and provide operating rules and the evaluated configuration.

sections.title: 4.1 Models and Operating Protocol
sections.content: We evaluate 7 model configurations on 2 world seeds, with one complete run per modelseed pair. We use GPT 6.1 Sol (Sol) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Opus) with high reasoning effort, and Kimi K3 (Kimi), GLM 5.2 (GLM), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 0910 (DeepSeek), GPT 6 Luna (Luna), and MiMo V2.6 Flash (MiMo) with max reasoning effort. Each run starts with 3,000 CNY, the same initial fleet, 2,141.83 CNY equipment-capital ceiling, and 15 CNY daily operating fee. Each evaluated season generates approximately 1,100 reservation requests. Agents receive the same business tools and instructions, fresh daily sessions, persistent records, and up to 200 model responses per day. Run and controller details appear in Appendix B. Runs within each seed share the initial shop and seeded external processes; their decisions then produce different fleets, obligations, and customer interactions. The main results table, value paths in Figure 1, and main-text process diagnostics average seed-level measurements equally across these worlds. Appendix reports individual outcomes for each modelseed pair. 4.2 Public-Information Rule Reference We also run Calendar, fixed operating policy, on both worlds. It uses twelve-product assortment with fixed prices, replenishment targets, maintenance, and recovery rules. Using public asset states, return estimates, and service schedules, it accepts bookings with positive estimated direct contribution and sufficient projected calendar capacity. Calendar allows one day for ordinary turnaround and interacts through agent-visible tools. It provides reference for the value of consistent routines. Appendix B.4 gives its operating rules. 4.3 Operating Outcomes At terminal day = 214, the score of solvent shop is ST = CT + LT ΛT , = ST V0, (3) where CT is cash, LT eligible equipment resale value, and ΛT outstanding liabilities, including refundable deposits and unearned reservation payments. We report value creation relative to the initial business value V0 = 3,397.06 CNY. Insolvency ends run with failure score. Model inference costs are recorded separately from business value; valuation details are in Appendix A.5. Reservation deliveries and reliability describe the business served. Reliability is deliveries divided by deliveries plus merchant-caused failures; ordinary customer cancellations are excluded.

sections.title: 4.4 Process Diagnostics
sections.content: We use four diagnostic families to relate operating outcomes to feasibility maintenance and resource valuation. All are computed from recorded states and actions without an LLM judge. Figure 4 reports equal-weight means across seeds, with ratios calculated within each run. Pending-booking gaps. After each days walkins, we check whether pending reservations have sufficient projected supply, using public asset states, service schedules, and return and delivery estimates. We report the share of observed booking days with shortage, both overall and one or two days before pickup. These rates track whether accepted bookings remain supported over time. Action-induced new gaps. We compare projected coverage immediately before and after supported action, counting calls that leave previously covered booking short. Rates are calculated 7 separately for each action type over relevant successful calls. Quotation calls can directly confirm bookings after customer approval, so they can also create projected gaps for existing commitments. Walk-in rentals use customer-trip batches instead. This check identifies subsequent choices that undermine the supply supporting existing commitments. Capital productivity. We measure net service contribution per 100 capital-CNY-days. Contribution includes rent and damage deductions, less service costs and estimated equipment-use consumption; the denominator accumulates occupied equipment capital, including inbound purchases. This describes the return generated by the resources tied up over time, complementing the official scores measure of total business value. Unrealized gains from capacity relaxation. At 40 fixed dates per run, we test whether slightly relaxing one products walk-in limit improves estimated contribution under conservative supply check. The test holds stock, prices, commitments, and that days customer demand fixed. We report how often positive estimated gain remains available under existing limits, and its mean across all sampled days, including zero-gain dates, using three-day turnaround allowance. Candidates depend on each runs fleet and existing limits, so the results describe remaining opportunities within that configuration. We therefore interpret these local estimates alongside the booking-gap rates. Full definitions, individual results, and counts appear together in Appendix D, following the same four-family order. Trajectory analysis connects these measurements to recorded information, executed choices, and subsequent outcomes. Matched bookings and selected historical-state probes provide further comparisons, documented in Appendix E.

sections.title: 5 Results and Analysis
sections.content: In this section, we compare agents long-term value creation and examine the resource-management patterns behind their performance. We focus on how agents maintain feasible plans and choose or revise resource allocations as opportunities change.

Choosing which commitments to make and retain. Accepting commitment ties up future capacity for an agreed return and limits which later opportunities can be pursued. Opus completes more bookings than Sol in both worlds without attaining comparable business value. Among 77 pairs of fully delivered bookings matched by customer request, equipment, quantities, rental dates, and promised service, it charges less in 75; total agreed rent on these pairs is 3037% lower than Sols. Its pricing records repeatedly recommend concessions after rejected quotes. Those commitments also shape later admission decisions. Two four-day table, chair, and cookware bookings earn CNY 33 each for Opus and CNY 60 for Sol; Opus later sets aside other offers because the cookware is committed. Its larger completed operation is therefore accompanied by weaker value capture from the equipment-time it commits. Appendix E.2.1 gives the paired transactions and pricing records; Appendix C.2 provides the full-run accounting. Once concrete conflict brings competing obligations into view, however, even agents with weaker overall returns or unstable schedules can weigh exit costs against the value of retaining booking. Facing two bookings that compete for sleeping bag and pad, DeepSeek compares their 10 rents, cancellation charges, and occupied time, then pays CNY 7.86 compensation before pickup to cancel the CNY 13.20 booking and preserve the CNY 73.50 booking, which is subsequently fulfilled. Similarly, when tent conflict cannot be resolved by rescheduling, Opus compares buying another tent against early cancellation and exits the booking. The larger difference lies in how consistently such comparisons shape commitments and resource allocations throughout the season. Both decisions are documented under Deliberate exit after economic comparison in Appendix E.2.1. Turning feedback and evaluations into resource reallocation. When resources are fully committed, acting on new opportunities requires revisiting existing allocations and previously evaluated alternatives. Sol and Luna can both assess alternative investments, but differ in how those assessments shape later resource decisions. In one shared world, Luna already holds higher-cost comfortchair model (about CNY 103 per unit) when it evaluates lower-cost comfort chair (about CNY 36) for expansion. It considers the candidates payback, delivery time, and an asset sale that could fund the purchase. About two weeks later, with nearly all capital committed, it reviews its highercost existing chair and supports retention through past rental income and continued earning potential. Luna mentions the lower-cost model as product it does not currently own, without revisiting the earlier funding proposal. Luna continues buying and selling other equipment, but purchases the lowercost comfort chairs more than two months after first assessing them. Sol, by contrast, repeatedly carries demand comparisons into allocation decisions. After reviewing recent demand, fleet sizes, delivery time, and holding costs, it buys sixth comfort chair rather than seventeenth lightweight chair. The lightweight fleet has earned more total rent, but the additional comfort chair would enable six-person comfortseating requests. Customer rejections of quoted lightweight-chair configurations prompt another adjustment: Sol checks that the remaining lightweight chairs cover near-term bookings, sells an unused chair, and buys another comfort chair once capital is released. As cold-weather demand weakens, Sol shifts from sleeping equipment to seating. Sol more consistently carries investment assessments into later decisions about which assets to retain and replace. Between Lunas initial assessment and eventual purchase, the shops receive walk-in requests for the same 141 comfort-chair units; Sol supplies 46 and Luna 16 under their respective fleets, prices, and capacity limits. Appendix E.2.2 documents the decision sequences and the scope of the walk-in and reservation comparisons. Using available capacity while protecting commitments. Future commitments require capacity at particular times, leaving intervening availability that may support additional work. In the MiMo and DeepSeek replays, many additional rentals would occupy equipment needed for upcoming bookings, leaving fewer opportunities that fit around the existing schedule. Figure 4D finds positive estimated contribution from small limit relaxation without new projected booking gap on an average of 31.25% of sampled days for Luna, compared with 12.50% for Sol. For Luna, they recur across products early and late in both seasons. sleeping-pad booking illustrates one way those opportunities are excluded. Luna blocks its ready three-person pad from walk-ins twelve days before pickup and keeps the restriction through the rental. In our capacity-relaxation test using the following days state, raising the limit by one unit admits an intervening rental scheduled to return week before pickup, with rent exceeding its estimated cleaning and usage costs. The restriction protects particular future use by closing much longer available interval. The case highlights the value of matching protection to the timing and capacity required by commitment. Unused opportunities also remain in both Sol runs. Appendix E.2.3 reports the rental intervals and local test results. Effective preparation for individual commitments does not consistently extend to joint feasibility, while more reliable fulfillment can coexist with weak returns and delayed resource reallocation. Sol more effectively compares competing uses of equipment and capital, and carries these comparisons into supply preparation and fleet changes. Its scheduling conflicts and unused rental opportunities expose limits in both feasibility maintenance and value comparison, even in the strongest runs.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced OutfitterBench to study how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing the value of resource allocations as opportunities change. Calendar outperforms several 11 LLM agents, while only the leading agent exceeds this fixed reference in both evaluated worlds. The trajectories reveal weaknesses both in sustaining feasible arrangements and in choosing worthwhile resource uses. Constraints correctly applied during preparation are sometimes omitted from later decisions. More reliable runs can still earn less from comparable bookings or delay capital reallocation. Feasibility maintenance and resource valuation are coupled. Existing commitments restrict subsequent uses, while alternative returns and adjustment costs guide which arrangements are worth retaining or revising. Paying to exit lower-value booking can preserve more valuable business, whereas replacing equipment can remove support for an existing obligation. Capacity-relaxation tests illustrate further trade-off: more precise protection can admit intervening rentals with positive estimated contribution while preserving projected booking coverage. Long-horizon consistency thus requires stable use of operating constraints and selective revision of commitments and allocations. These findings motivate testing decision support that combines dependable constraint checks with selective economic reassessment. Such support could link proposed changes to affected commitments and retain evaluated alternatives with the conditions that would make them worth revisiting. OutfitterBench provides testbed for studying how agents maintain feasible plans while choosing and revising resource uses for long-term value.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: The environment draws on real product and weather records, but customer behavior is rule-based rather than LLM-driven, and costs and operating events follow simulation assumptions. Transfer to other markets or real operations remains untested. With only two world seeds and one run per modelseed pair, the stability of the observed rankings under broader sampling remains uncertain. Diagnostics and selected cases help interpret decisions without isolating each behaviors contribution to the final score; capacity-relaxation tests do not follow subsequent agent decisions and thus do not estimate additional seasonal profit. We use fixed business tools and daily-session controller, without general-purpose shell such as Bash or coding-agent harnesses such as Codex or Claude Code.
